title: When Leaders Reduce Their Status, People Tell Them the Truth
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using Boston Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla, who plays rough pickup basketball with his assistants, the post argues that leaders get more candor when they shrink the status gap between themselves and their team. The pickup games produce teasing and camaraderie that make assistants more willing to debate him during the season. The author claims that position, authority and title discourage people from challenging a leader who can reward and punish. Leaders cannot erase status entirely, but visibly setting it aside invites people to engage as peers without crossing lines. The result is more honest answers, faster decisions and a safer, more collaborative environment.
points: Mazzulla's pickup games with his assistants deliberately lower implicit status to invite open debate.
Status of position and title suppresses challenge because leaders control rewards and punishments.
Because status can never be fully removed, reducing it invites collegial candor without disrespect.
Leaders who lead with influence rather than authority get more honest answers and quicker, better decisions.
quotes: Boston Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla is willing to get physically bruised to prove he wants an open forum of discussion and debate with his assistant coaches.
Any time a leader reduces or casts aside their status, they encourage more openness and honest feedback from those they lead.
Team members are less likely to challenge or question the views of leaders who have the status to reward and punish them.
Any time a leader levels the playing field by reducing their status, they essentially ask others to engage them in critical discussions as they would peers.
Leaders who push status aside get more honest answers to their questions and more candid ideas in discussions.
Minimizing leadership status creates a different conversation between leaders and team members, one that is more spontaneous, outspoken, and safe.
